title: Ki Tisa: the thirteen attributes (Exodus 34:6–7)
hookLine: "The LORD, the LORD, God, merciful and gracious, long-suffering", chanted on holy days

cards: On a festival morning, as the doors of the ark open and the Torah scroll is about to come out, some congregations stop and sing the same words three times over.

On Yom Kippur the words return again and again, through the day, until the closing service. No rabbi composed them. They come from Exodus: the words Moses heard in the cleft of the rock, as God passed by.
Moses asked to see. What he got was something to hear.

teach.b: Moses has carved two new tablets and climbed back up the mountain. God descends in the cloud, passes before him, and calls out.
In the JPS 1917 translation: "The LORD, the LORD, God, merciful and gracious, long-suffering, and abundant in goodness and truth."
It goes on: keeping mercy to the thousandth generation, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin.
Jewish tradition counts these as the thirteen attributes of mercy; commentators divide the phrases in slightly different ways, but the count of thirteen holds.

teach.h: GOD SHOWS AN ORDER OF PRAYER.
teach.b: The Talmud, in Rosh Hashanah, imagines God here wrapped in a prayer shawl like a leader of the service, showing Moses an order of prayer, and saying: whenever Israel sins, let them say this before Me, and I will forgive.
So after the golden calf, the people are given words to come back with.

teach.h: AS GOD IS MERCIFUL, SO BE YOU.
teach.b: In the synagogue, there's a twist. In the Torah, verse seven goes on to say God will by no means clear the guilty. The prayer stops mid-sentence, just before that line, so it ends on the word for clearing, for cleansing.
The Talmud, in Yoma, reads the verse's two halves together: God clears those who return, and does not clear those who don't.
And another Talmudic passage, in Shabbat, reads these qualities as a pattern for people: as God is gracious and merciful, so you be gracious and merciful.

how: The thirteen attributes are chanted when the ark is opened on festivals in some communities, throughout the Selichot prayers before the High Holy Days, on fast days, and again and again on Yom Kippur.

o: when you lift up: the portion of the thirteen attributes
the prayer sung three times as the ark is opened
merciful and gracious, the first of God's qualities

games.q: what's inside the attributes — tap the pairs.
p: God shows an order of prayer
as God is merciful, so be you

s: the thirteen attributes were composed by rabbis
they're Exodus 34:6–7, the words Moses heard as God passed by.
in the synagogue, the verse is cut off before 'by no means clear the guilty'
the prayer ends on v'nakeh, the word for clearing.
everyone counts the thirteen the same way
commentators divide the phrases in slightly different ways; the number thirteen is tradition.

games.q: you're a rabbi turning Exodus 34:6–7 into a prayer. the verse goes on: and that will by no means clear the guilty. what do you do?
o: stop just before that line, on the word for clearing.
replace it with a new line.
games.why: the prayer stops mid-verse, on v'nakeh, clearing. the people are given words to come back with, and the words end on forgiveness.

practice: Let the list pass slowly through your mind: merciful, gracious, slow to anger, abundant in kindness, true, forgiving.
Pick the one you've had least of lately, and picture meeting one person who tests it, a child, a coworker, yourself, with that quality, just once.
If you pray, you can say the opening words as they're written; if not, just hold the word you chose.

wordCard.voice: Ki Tisa. The portion where Moses hears the thirteen attributes of mercy: merciful and gracious, slow to anger, abundant in goodness and truth.

orig.note: Hebrew: merciful and gracious, from the thirteen attributes of mercy.

carryVoice: Your line: merciful and gracious. Something to call on, and something to copy. Day three hundred sixty-seven.
